body_markdown:
People from all walks of life dream about sliding back a large wooden door, wiping away some dust, and pushing out an old vehicle that had been sitting for decades. Even the worst long-hiding hulk of a car or motorcycle has some value—at least to a mechanically gifted dreamer. When the right person finds the right machine, the results can be fascinating to watch, and thanks to the internet it’s never been easier to enjoy these moments.


The latest example is Matt Walksler of the Wheels Through Time Museum in Maggie Valley, North Carolina. It’s the spot to go find out if you love old American motorcycles. Matt and his crew not only display cool vintage machines, but also restore and maintain even more. The most recent engine project to come across the bench is a 1946 Harley-Davidson Knucklehead, but thanks to their expertise, the right parts and tools on hand, and the magic of editing, this engine[only takes 40 minutes](https://youtu.be/iqVBq9ngtrA?si=nKudn1BRlFAKmZ1C) to completely rebuild the right way.


The motorcycle itself was a barn find, and their first impressions of the engine are positive, but it doesn’t take long to find a few surprises. Matt points out during disassembly that many of the engine parts appear untouched, like the hardware that holds the cylinders to the case. Items like these usually get even slightly mangled when the engine gets disassembled the first, third, or potentially more times. This is, after all, an eight-decade-old motorcycle engine.


Turns out all those small signs that were hinting at an untouched engine were merely red herrings. While there were many factory-fit Harley-Davidson parts still present and usable inside the engine, the pistons and cylinders were not two of them. After popping off the cylinder heads, Matt and his crew find the rear cylinder has been machined and fitted with a piston 70 thousandths of an inch larger in diameter. The front piston is 60 thousandths larger and has a broken piston ring along with the carbon buildup that follows such a break.


The cylinder heads get reworked on their own bench.


Wheels Through Time


The engine came out of the motorcycle a while ago, but still needed to be rebuilt.


Wheels Through Time


It might be a little crusty, but Matt thinks it’s got potential.


Wheels Through Time


Once everything is taken apart and the cleaning completed, the real fun can begin. The mix of new and restored parts combines to create a fresh engine. If a person is used to multi-cylinder automotive engines, a Knucklehead looks comically simple. In some ways it is, but during assembly, Matt expertly calls out the intriguing nuances and fine adjustments that come with rebuilding items that were initially built when precision machining was more expensive and challenging than it is today.


The cylinder heads took a little more work to assemble correctly, but seeing the engine become a black, chrome, and bare aluminum beast ready to power a motorcycle is to watch an artist at work. Would it be this fun if I were doing it myself? Likely not. Watching people who are truly in their element makes any project an entertaining occasion. Going along for the ride on this rebuild with Matt doesn’t completely replace getting out in my own shop, but learning a few new things while working vicariously is always a good time. After all, who knows when I might need to rebuild an 80-year-old Harley-Davidson Knucklehead?
